title.en: Distinguish text files and binary files

say.en: You type the marks of 60 students into a program, close it, and everything is gone. Files keep data on the disk so the program can use it again tomorrow. In this lesson: Explain why files are needed.
Distinguish text files and binary files.
Recognise common file types.

body.en: Variables live in main memory (RAM) and are lost when the program ends. A file is a named location on secondary storage that stores data permanently. Python programs themselves are stored in *files* with the .py extension. File handling lets a program store its input and output data and reuse it later.

points.en: Each file has a name and location (path)
Programs read input from and write output to *files*

narration.en: A text file stores each number as characters, one byte per digit plus a separator, and any editor can read it. A binary file stores each whole number in a fixed 4 bytes, as the computer holds it in memory: smaller for big numbers, but unreadable without the program. Store 1000 six-digit numbers. Which file is smaller? With 2-digit numbers, which wins now?

title.en: On the board: Why files, and text versus binary

say.en: Variables live in RAM. When the program ends, they are gone.
A file on secondary storage keeps the data permanently, so another run of the program can read it back.
A text file stores characters as codes. Hello World followed by newline is stored as 72, 101, 108 and so on; each line ends with backslash n.
A binary file stores raw bytes, like an image or a sound. It looks like nonsense in a text editor and needs the right program.

narration.en: We see why data in variables is lost and data in files is kept, then look at the bytes inside a text file.

say.en: We see why data in variables is lost and data in files is kept, then look at the bytes inside a text file.

prompt.en: Sort each file by its type.

explanation.en: Text files hold characters in lines ending with \n and open in any text editor. Binary files hold bytes that are not characters (images, audio, video, programs, pickled objects); a text editor shows garbage.
explanation.kn: ಪಠ್ಯ ಕಡತದಲ್ಲಿ ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳ ಸಾಲುಗಳು; ಬೈನರಿ ಕಡತದಲ್ಲಿ ಅಕ್ಷರವಲ್ಲದ ಬೈಟ್‌ಗಳು (ಚಿತ್ರ, ಧ್ವನಿ, ಪ್ರೋಗ್ರಾಂ).

say.en: Text file or binary file? Sort each file by its type.

body.en: A text file is a sequence of characters: letters, digits and symbols stored as ASCII or Unicode codes. Each line ends with an end-of-line (EOL) character, newline \n by default, and the file can be opened in any text editor. A binary file stores bytes that do not represent characters, such as images, audio, video, compressed and executable *files*. Opening one in a text editor shows garbage, and a single wrong bit can corrupt it.

points.en: Both are stored on disk as 0s and 1s

heading.en: CSV Files and File Handling Practice

tagline.en: CSV files and the csv module: writer, writerow, writerows, reader, newline and delimiter, followed by mixed board questions across text, binary and CSV files.

myth.en: csv.reader gives me back the numbers I wrote, so row[2] + 5 works.

truth.en: A CSV file is text, so every value read back is a str. Convert with int() or float() before doing arithmetic; row[2] + 5 raises TypeError. The writer accepted ints, so learners expect ints back. The file only stores characters; the type information is lost.

say.en: CSV is a text format: one row per line, values separated by a delimiter (comma by default).
Open with newline=""; write with csv.writer(f).writerow() / writerows().
csv.reader(f) gives each row as a list of strings; use next() to skip a header.
Convert numbers read from CSV with int() / float().
Text file: no module; binary objects: pickle; tables: csv.

explain.en: Pickle keeps Python types, CSV keeps tables readable by other programs, and plain text files hold free-form text.

takeaway.en: CSV is a text format: one row per line, values separated by a delimiter (comma by default).

narration.en: Many people think: csv.reader gives me back the numbers I wrote, so row[2] + 5 works. Actually: A CSV file is text, so every value read back is a str. Convert with int() or float() before doing arithmetic; row[2] + 5 raises TypeError. The writer accepted ints, so learners expect ints back. The file only stores characters; the type information is lost.

problem.en: Classify each file as text or binary: report.txt, marks.csv, prog.py, selfie.jpg, song.mp3, setup.exe

steps.en: report.txt, marks.csv and prog.py contain characters only, so they are text files.
selfie.jpg (image) and song.mp3 (audio) store encoded bytes: binary.

answer.en: Text: report.txt, marks.csv, prog.py. Binary: selfie.jpg, song.mp3, setup.exe.

narration.en: Six files from your own computer. Sort them into text and binary.

say.en: Six files from your own computer. Sort them into text and binary. Classify each file as text or binary: report.txt, marks.csv, prog.py, selfie.jpg, song.mp3, setup.exe.
report.txt, marks.csv and prog.py contain characters only, so they are text files.
selfie.jpg image and song.mp3 audio store encoded bytes: binary.
setup.exe holds machine instructions: binary.
So the answer is Text: report.txt, marks.csv, prog.py. Binary: selfie.jpg, song.mp3, setup.exe.
